title: Community Engagement With an Honest Account of Influence
audience: All staff; useful for supervisors and people planning engagement.
filename: courses/One DSD - I15 - Community Engagement With an Honest Account of Influence.pptx

slides.text:
One DSD People, Access and Culture
Community Engagement With an Honest Account of Influence
Examine what people can shape, what participation requires, and how their input reaches an actual decision.
Intermediate self-directed learning
slides.narration: Engagement is a relationship with a purpose, not simply a meeting or a list of names. People deserve to know what they are being asked to contribute and what can change as a result. This course follows fictional service and workplace decisions while examining access, timing, influence, and a useful report-back. You will compare different forms of involvement without assuming that every invitation shares decision authority. The central question is whether the promise matches the actual opportunity.

slides.text:
An invitation before or after the choice
Imagine being asked to help shape an onboarding guide after its content has already been settled. What can your contribution still change?

An honest invitation names the remaining question. A useful review can occur after a decision, but it should not be described as shared design of a choice that is closed.
slides.narration: People can make valuable contributions at different stages, but those stages offer different influence. A review after an introduction may help improve later use. That is different from choosing the design before it is settled. The invitation should explain what remains open and what is constrained. Consider a fictional experience where the request promises more influence than it offers. The problem is not that every decision must be shared; it is that people need a truthful account of the role they are being offered.

slides.text:
Different depths of participation
Informing explains. Seeking input asks for a response. Shared design involves people in shaping alternatives. Shared decision-making includes actual authority.

Each can be useful when named accurately. Attendance, an advisory title, or a distribution list does not establish the depth of the relationship.
slides.narration: The familiar word partnership can hide important differences. Someone who receives updates has a different role from someone who develops an alternative, and both differ from someone authorized to make the decision. Name the actual contribution rather than use the strongest label available. This lets participants decide whether the invitation fits their interests and circumstances. It also makes an account of the work more accurate, because a large contact list cannot by itself demonstrate that varied experience shaped a choice.

slides.text:
Two communication designs still open
A fictional service team compares two ways to explain a response process. Both designs can still change.

Invite people to examine complete alternatives and explain the choice they can influence. Repeatedly asking only after decisions are fixed may preserve existing power while creating the appearance of shared design.
slides.narration: Here the improved approach connects participation to something tangible. People can see the actual explanation, compare its route, and describe what helps or remains unclear. Staff should make constraints and actual decision authority visible without inventing a promise. If feedback changes an alternative, that influence can be explained later. The example also shows a possible systemic mechanism: repeated late invitations may keep the same people shaping options. Whether that occurs in a real setting requires evidence about timing and actual decisions.

slides.text:
Comparing two service explanations
Two fictional service explanations remain open. Which invitation best supports meaningful input?
A. Explain the alternatives, constraints, and what participant input can change.
B. Ask participants to endorse the version staff prefer.
C. Describe a shared decision even though staff retain the actual authority.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: A fictional team is comparing two service explanations before choosing a recommendation. Both alternatives can still change, but staff retain the actual decision responsibility. Participants will need clear information and usable communication to examine the choice. Consider how each invitation describes the influence available and what may happen if that description becomes a repeated practice. An impressive label does not supply authority, and attendance does not establish influence. Choose the invitation that respects people's time by making the purpose, constraints, and possible contribution understandable.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Explain the alternatives, constraints, and what participant input can change.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Ask participants to endorse the version staff prefer.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Describe a shared decision even though staff retain the actual authority.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
Participants can examine the real choice and decide whether to contribute. Keep the promise within actual authority.

Can a participant explain what their contribution may change?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This invitation connects the contribution to actual alternatives and makes constraints visible. Participants can judge the opportunity and examine the complete designs. If input changes a feature, staff can later explain that influence. The process still needs appropriate communication support and honest limits; a clear invitation alone does not establish that every affected person was reached or heard.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
An endorsement request can be legitimate if named honestly, but it is not shared design of open alternatives.

Can a participant explain what their contribution may change?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Seeking endorsement is different from inviting people to shape alternatives. If staff present their preferred version as the only meaningful answer, participants may have little room to identify another concern. Repeated use can preserve existing decision patterns while being described as engagement. Name the actual request and consider what choice remains open before presenting it as shared design.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Overstating authority can create false expectations. The depth of participation should match the real decision route.

Can a participant explain what their contribution may change?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: People may value contributing even when they do not hold decision authority. Claiming a shared decision where it does not exist undermines that choice. Explain who decides and what input can influence in ordinary language. The stronger relationship comes from an accurate promise rather than a more impressive label, with evidence of how the contribution reached the work.

slides.text:
Who is affected and who is invited
A familiar partner list may not include the range of people affected. Some invited participants may still be unable to use the response route.

Examine the relationship between the decision and the experience sought. Do not ask one person to stand for everyone who shares an identity or service connection.
slides.narration: A long list can be a useful starting point, but it should not end the inquiry. The question is whose experience matters to this decision and who has a meaningful way to contribute. People outside established networks may face different barriers. Those on the list may also be unable to prepare or respond. A culture brief can suggest questions and possible relationships, while actual dialogue reveals experience. Describe the reach honestly instead of treating familiar participation as full representation.

slides.text:
Preparation that makes choices understandable
Participants need enough clear information to examine the question. Explain the purpose, alternatives, constraints, and intended use of input.

Use appropriate language and accessible formats. A large background packet cannot substitute for a clear account of what people are being asked to consider.
slides.narration: Good preparation respects people's time and knowledge. It makes the actual task understandable without assuming they know internal terminology. Complete alternatives are often more useful than a slogan about the proposed change. Participants should be able to see what is open and what remains a requirement. Appropriate communication support may also be needed. The aim is not to disclose every organizational detail, but to provide the material people need for an informed contribution within actual information boundaries.

slides.text:
Participation has costs
Time, travel, communication support, preparation, and other conditions can affect who participates. Some burdens are less visible inside an office.

Discuss feasible arrangements through the appropriate process. Do not promise payment or resources without authority, and do not assume willingness means participation has no cost.
slides.narration: People may value the opportunity and still face substantial effort to take part. An invitation that ignores those conditions can repeatedly favor participants with more available time or established support. Ask what the task involves and what arrangements are possible through the relevant process. Compensation and resources have real responsibilities that this course does not approve. A respectful request is clear about what is offered, what is uncertain, and how the contribution will be used, rather than assuming that gratitude replaces support.

slides.text:
The person's direction and chosen support
A family member may contribute important experience. The person using a service may want help, direct participation, or another arrangement.

Keep the person's purpose and chosen support visible. Family input should not automatically replace their own voice or be treated as evidence that everyone shares the same preference.
slides.narration: Relationships can strengthen participation when the arrangement fits the person's choice and the actual process. Someone may want a relative to explain part of the experience or help compare alternatives. They may also want to speak directly about something different. Clarify the roles without imposing a single model of independence or family involvement. A community brief can prepare this question but cannot settle it. The resulting account should distinguish whose perspective was offered and what it concerned.

slides.text:
Staff input with a truthful promise
A team asks employees to co-design onboarding after the new guide is fixed. Staff can still identify problems in use, but cannot choose its initial content.

Explain the real review opportunity or reopen a defined choice through the appropriate authority. Repeated overstated invitations can weaken trust and hide whose input shapes workplace practice.
slides.narration: This workplace example uses the same reasoning as the service case. Employees deserve to know whether they are reviewing use, developing alternatives, or sharing a decision. A closed initial design does not make later feedback worthless. It means the invitation should accurately name the stage and the question. Across onboarding and development, overstated promises can affect willingness to contribute. Examine what changed in response to input before describing the process as collaborative, and keep decisions within their actual authority.

slides.text:
Employee input after an onboarding decision
The onboarding guide is final, but staff are invited to co-design it. Which response is most honest?
A. Keep the label because employees are attending.
B. Name a genuine review question, or establish an open choice through the proper authority.
C. Cancel all staff feedback because the first version is fixed.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: A fictional DSD team has finished an onboarding guide. The planned meeting invitation asks employees to co-design it, although the first version is already fixed. Staff may still identify problems in use or inform a later revision. Consider how to preserve that useful learning without promising a choice that is not currently open. Repeated overstated invitations could affect willingness to contribute throughout the employee life cycle. The strongest response makes the actual stage and question clear and keeps any reopening of a decision within the appropriate authority.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Keep the label because employees are attending.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. Name a genuine review question, or establish an open choice through the proper authority.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. Cancel all staff feedback because the first version is fixed.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Attendance does not establish shared design. The invitation should explain what is actually open.

What remains open, and does the invitation say so?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: Calling the activity co-design because employees attend hides the difference between a closed decision and an open choice. People may expect their contribution to shape something that is already settled. Repeated promises of this kind can weaken trust across onboarding and development. Examine what can still change and describe that opportunity accurately before asking for staff time.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
A later review can be useful when the promise is accurate. Do not imply authority or an open decision that has not been established.

What remains open, and does the invitation say so?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This response preserves useful participation while correcting the promise. Staff may examine how the guide works, identify unclear steps, or help shape a future revision if that opportunity genuinely exists. If a design choice is to be reopened, the proper authority must establish it. The invitation should name the actual question and how input will be considered.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
A fixed first version does not make future learning pointless. The issue is an overstated invitation.

What remains open, and does the invitation say so?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: A fixed version can still be examined in use, and staff may notice something important for a later decision. Canceling all feedback would confuse a limit on present authority with a lack of value in experience. Offer the real opportunity honestly, with an appropriate report-back, rather than implying either unlimited influence or no possible contribution.

slides.text:
Listening to experience and examining the task
An account can reveal a burden that staff overlooked. Ask how it connects to the specific choice, without requiring a private history.

Different accounts may point to different needs. Compare them with the actual process and relevant evidence rather than assuming one story supplies a complete answer.
slides.narration: Listening is more than collecting a quotation. It involves understanding what the person says about a particular interaction or condition and how that relates to the work. A participant may identify a confusing handoff while another values the same route for different reasons. Both can inform alternatives. Avoid pressing for personal details merely to make the account more compelling. The contribution should remain with the scope the person agreed to share and should be considered alongside other appropriate evidence.

slides.text:
A contribution that reaches the comparison
Show how input changes an option, identifies a concern, or supports a reason for keeping part of the design.

A thank-you alone does not explain influence. Some suggestions may not be adopted; describe the relevant reasons without implying that the contributor's experience was invalid.
slides.narration: Not every useful contribution produces the requested change. A suggestion may conflict with an actual requirement, address a different task, or reveal a tradeoff that needs further consideration. The important step is an understandable connection between input and the comparison. Explain which alternative changed and why, or what concern remains. This account lets participants examine whether their contribution has been understood. It should not present disagreement as a failure of partnership or claim that accepting one suggestion resolves all concerns.

slides.text:
Clear responsibilities without false authority
People need to know who can decide and what staff can realistically promise. Learning activities do not transfer agency authority.

Name the relevant boundary in ordinary language. Where a decision or resource is uncertain, seek appropriate guidance instead of describing a shared power that has not been established.
slides.narration: A warm invitation can still be precise. You can explain that participants are helping compare a communication design while the responsible role retains the decision. You can also acknowledge that some requirements cannot be changed through this activity. Clarity protects the relationship because people can judge whether the offered influence is meaningful. This course does not create a new board, process, timetable, or role. It asks that the description of participation fit the actual authority and the question being considered.

slides.text:
Report back with something people can examine
Return the relevant choice, reasons, and limits in a usable form. Explain what happened to the input and what remains open.

Protect private material and respect acknowledgment preferences. A complete report-back is about the defined task; it need not claim that all future questions are closed.
slides.narration: A useful return gives participants more than assurance that staff listened. It provides enough appropriate material to recognize their contribution in the actual result. That may include revised wording, an explanation of the comparison, and unresolved questions. Share within the relevant information boundaries and ask about credit preferences where appropriate. The account should be neither a celebration that erases limits nor an endless promise of participation. It should explain what the defined task established and what it did not.

slides.text:
Acknowledgment is not universal agreement
One participant says the revised message reflects their concern. Another has not replied. Those are different facts.

Record the actual responses without treating silence as approval or one positive comment as a population outcome. The report-back may be complete while the use of the design remains untested.
slides.narration: A participant's recognition is valuable evidence about whether a contribution was represented. It does not automatically establish agreement with every part of a decision or prove that the service now works for everyone. A missing reply also cannot establish satisfaction or disinterest. Keep the question each response answered visible. The next useful inquiry may concern actual use of the material. Honest distinctions allow progress to be described without requiring either an exaggerated success claim or a dismissal of the work already completed.

slides.text:
A positive reply and a missing reply
One participant says the revised message reflects their concern. Another has not replied. How should the account describe the result?
A. Everyone supports the decision because nobody objected.
B. The service outcome improved for all participants.
C. One concern was recognized in the revision; other views and actual-use effects remain unknown.
In Slide Show view, select a response to explore its effects.
slides.narration: A fictional comparison has ended, and staff return the revised service message with an explanation of the choice. One contributor replies that their concern is represented. Another has not answered. There is no evidence of the message's actual use in services yet. Consider what these facts establish and what they leave unknown. An honest report can acknowledge a useful contribution without claiming universal support or a service outcome. Choose the account that distinguishes the completed task, the particular response received, and the questions still open.

links.name: Answer 1
links.text: A. Everyone supports the decision because nobody objected.

links.name: Answer 2
links.text: B. The service outcome improved for all participants.

links.name: Answer 3
links.text: C. One concern was recognized in the revision; other views and actual-use effects remain unknown.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Silence does not establish support. Report the response actually received and the missing information.

What question did the actual response answer?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: An absent objection cannot establish agreement, especially when one participant has not replied. The person may not have seen the message or may have other reasons for silence. Report the actual response and the missing information. Repeatedly treating silence as approval can conceal whose concerns remain unheard, so an honest account should preserve that uncertainty.

slides.text:
Consider the possible effects
Recognition of wording does not establish a service outcome. Actual use and effects require further evidence.

What question did the actual response answer?
Try another response
Continue learning
slides.narration: The participant has said something about the revised message and their contribution. They have not supplied evidence about the later service experience of everyone affected. Turning that reply into an outcome claim reaches beyond its scope. A useful report distinguishes the completed comparison and return account from the separate question of whether the design works in actual use.

slides.text:
Why this response helps
This keeps the useful contribution visible without converting a limited reply into universal agreement or a later outcome.

What question did the actual response answer?
Continue learning
Try another response
slides.narration: This account acknowledges progress without claiming more than is known. One contributor recognizes their concern in the revision, another view is absent, and later use remains unexamined. Those facts can coexist. Keep the defined task and future question separate, so the relationship offers a clear account rather than either an exaggerated success story or a dismissal of useful work.

slides.text:
How recurring invitations distribute influence
Timing, information, access, and familiar networks can repeatedly determine who shapes alternatives and who only reacts afterward.

Trace the route from invitation to contribution to decision. Examine actual opportunities and consequences before making a finding about inequity.
slides.narration: The systemic mechanism lies in the repeated arrangement, not simply in a meeting label. If only familiar organizations receive early information and accessible preparation, their ideas may define the options everyone else later sees. That possibility should be examined against actual invitation routes and decision records. Other explanations and constraints may matter. A revised approach should be assessed for whether new contributions influence choices, rather than counted as successful because more people attended or more messages were sent.

slides.text:
Evidence of an honest relationship
Compare what was promised, what participants could use, how input was considered, and what was returned.

Distinguish reach, attendance, influence, and later effects. People can value a conversation while still identifying an unresolved service barrier or a limit on the decision.
slides.narration: These distinctions create a more useful evidence account. A delivered invitation shows reach. Attendance shows presence. A documented change linked to input shows something about influence. Later experience with the revised service addresses another question. None should stand in automatically for the others. Participants' accounts can help staff understand missing links while appropriate records clarify the decision route. The aim is to learn what the relationship actually made possible, with privacy and uncertainty preserved.

slides.text:
Rewrite an overstated invitation
Privately revise this fictional message: 'Help us design the new guide. The final version has already been approved.'

Name the actual opportunity and what can change. If no choice is open, describe information sharing or a later review honestly instead of promising shared design.
slides.narration: This reflection keeps the relationship useful without disguising its limits. You might invite feedback on the guide's use if that is genuinely open, explaining how concerns will be considered. If a defined design choice can be reopened, the appropriate authority needs to establish that opportunity first. The rewritten invitation should match what staff can actually offer. Notice how the change respects participants' time and gives them a clearer basis for deciding whether to contribute.

slides.text:
Engagement across learning and workplace stages
Community learning can deepen service practice. Employee input can improve onboarding, development, and transitions when its influence is clear.

Recognize expertise without assigning representative duties from identity. Use briefs to prepare questions and appropriate relationships to learn from varied experience.
slides.narration: The course applies inside and outside the division without making the two settings identical. A new colleague may notice an unwritten rule that experienced staff no longer see. A person using a service may identify a burdensome step that looks minor from an office. Both contributions deserve a truthful account of what they can shape. Neither person must speak for an entire identity group. Continued learning comes from clear questions, usable participation, and evidence of how the contribution reached the work.

slides.text:
Make the promise match the opportunity
Name what is open, support usable participation, and show how input reaches the actual decision.

Return an honest account with appropriate limits. When a repeated arrangement narrows influence, investigate the route and its effects rather than treating participation counts as the whole relationship.
slides.narration: Meaningful engagement does not require exaggerating the authority available. It requires a clear purpose, respectful preparation, and an honest connection between contributions and the work. People can help staff examine service decisions and workplace practices when they know what their input can change. Continue distinguishing reach from influence and a report-back from a later outcome. That approach helps build dependable relationships while keeping the actual responsibilities, evidence, and unanswered questions visible.

outcomes: Clarify what people can shape before inviting their participation.
Compare ways to include people whose experience is missing.
Recognize participation costs, access needs, and the value of community expertise.
Explain how input affected the choice and what could not change.
